summary: In the hall, Agent Brown kneels beside the body on the floor and checks his vital signs, then reports, "He's gone." Standing over him, Agent Smith smiles and says, "Good-bye, Mr. Anderson."

what_changes.before: Checking the body's vital signs without having reported a result
what_changes.evidence: Kneeling beside him, Agent Brown checks his vital signs. AGENT BROWN He's gone.

what_changes.after: Smiles and bids farewell to the dead man: "Good-bye, Mr. Anderson."
what_changes.evidence: Agent Smith smiles, standing over him. AGENT SMITH Good-bye, Mr. Anderson.

event_hint.one_line: Agents confirm Neo's death in the hall and Smith dismisses him.

minds.wants: To complete the assigned verification and report the result cleanly to his superior, closing out the operation.
minds.feels: A flat, procedural certainty. He is the instrument that confirms; there is no investment in the outcome beyond its accuracy, which is itself a kind of coldness.
minds.shows: Only the report — "He's gone." He lets nothing else be seen, which is the whole of him.
minds.basis: He is the one told to "Check him" in sc-210, and here he kneels, checks vital signs, and delivers a terse factual verdict. His entire contribution is two words of confirmed fact, matching the pattern of an Agent who performs a function without affect.

believes_about.belief: That Smith is the lead and that reporting the confirmation to him is the correct protocol.
That the man on the floor is dead and the matter is settled — that his verification is final.
believes_about.wrong_because: The event's shape is a death-and-resurrection; this confirmation of death is about to be undone, so Brown's certainty that the case is closed is precisely wrong.

minds.wants: To savor and formally punctuate his victory — to turn a kill into a ceremony of dismissal.
minds.feels: Triumph, and something closer to relish than mere satisfaction. The smile and the use of the man's real name signal a personal, almost intimate, closing of an account rather than a bureaucratic one.
minds.shows: A smile and a courteous farewell — "Good-bye, Mr. Anderson." The politeness is the cruelty; he lets the pleasure of winning show precisely because it costs him nothing to display it over a corpse.
minds.basis: In sc-210 he stands over the fallen Neo and orders the check, taking no chances — the dominance is already established. Here, once confirmation arrives, he does not merely accept it; he smiles and addresses the dead man by name, a performative farewell that exceeds what the task requires.

believes_about.belief: That Neo is finished — a problem permanently solved, worth a final, dismissive courtesy.
believes_about.wrong_because: This is exactly the mistake the death-and-resurrection structure is built to punish: the farewell is premature, and the man he is dismissing is about to return.

believes_about.belief: That Brown's confirmation can be trusted as the closing word on the operation.
believes_about.wrong_because: The confirmation is real but incomplete — it will shortly be invalidated by Neo's revival, so Smith's trust in it as a final verdict is misplaced.

connects_back: Smith's command "Check him" in sc-210, which this scene answers with the completed check.
The three chest wounds that felled Neo in sc-210, the physical cause of the death Brown now confirms.
The flatline on the life monitors in sc-209, the off-site confirmation that mirrors Brown's on-site verdict.
Trinity holding Neo's body in sc-211, the counter-action happening in parallel that will undo what is declared here.
sets_up: The reversal in which Neo's confirmed death is overturned and he returns (ev-034).
Smith's coming defeat when the dismissed man passes through him and he explodes (ev-034).
The crew's escape from the breached hovercraft via the EMP and Neo's unplugging (ev-035).
dramatic_function: It is the false closure of the death-and-resurrection arc — the moment the story lets the antagonists believe they have won, so that the reversal lands with maximum force. The ceremony of dismissal makes the victory feel complete, which is exactly what the resurrection must then shatter.
